notes.meaning: The second lot drawn at Shiloh gave land to the tribe of Simeon. Their towns sat entirely inside the larger territory of Judah. Long before, Jacob had warned that Simeon would be scattered among the other tribes because of his past violence (Genesis 49:7). God kept that word while still giving them a place to live.

The list starts with settlements in the dry southern desert called the Negev. Beersheba was famous as the home of Abraham and Isaac, where they dug wells and worshiped the Lord. These small desert towns were handed over from Judah to give Simeon room to settle.

More southern towns are named here, finishing a group of thirteen cities and their outlying villages. Hormah was an old battleground from the wilderness years, and Ziklag later became a safe refuge for David. Even though these towns were tucked away in the dry south, God provided them as real homes for Simeon's families.

Four additional towns are given to Simeon, including Ain and Rimmon. Some of these sat in the southern desert, while others lay in the western foothills. Because these towns were separated, Simeon never held one single, connected piece of land.

Simeon received the open villages around these towns all the way south to Baalath-beer. This southern Ramah marked the outer edge of their territory in the Negev. The record confirms that all these scattered settlements made up the full share for the clans of Simeon.

Judah had received more land than its people could use, so some of it was given to Simeon. When the leaders realized this, Judah gave up the extra towns without fighting or arguing. God's people show true love when they share freely with brothers and sisters in need.

The third lot drawn at Shiloh went to the tribe of Zebulun. Zebulun was younger than his brother Issachar, but his lot was drawn first, matching Jacob's old blessing. The southern boundary of their new territory began at the town of Sarid.

From Sarid, Zebulun's border ran westward toward the Mediterranean Sea and reached the stream near Jokneam. Even though other tribes touched the shoreline, this land gave Zebulun easy access to coastal trade. This helped fulfill Jacob's ancient promise that Zebulun would look out toward the sea.

Starting again at Sarid, the boundary line turned eastward past Mount Tabor toward Daberath and Japhia. It then crossed over to Gath-hepher, which later became famous as the home of the prophet Jonah. From there, the border continued along the hills to Rimmon and Neah.

The boundary curved north around Neah to the town of Hannathon. It finally came to an end at the valley of Iphtah-el, marking the northern edge of Zebulun's land. This set the borders around the quiet hill country of Lower Galilee.

Several more towns are named, including Shimron and Bethlehem. This Bethlehem was a northern village in Galilee, not the town in Judah where Jesus was born. In all, Zebulun held twelve cities and their villages, giving them a small but fruitful home.

The fourth lot at Shiloh was drawn for the tribe of Issachar. Their land was divided among their family clans, just as God had commanded. They were placed right next to their brother tribe Zebulun, keeping the two families close.

Issachar received the wide, fertile plain of Jezreel, including towns like Shunem. Jezreel later became a royal residence for Israel's kings, while Shunem was the hometown of the kind woman who sheltered the prophet Elisha. Although parts of the valley were swampy and hard to clear at first, the rich soil was a wonderful gift.

More towns of Issachar are listed, including Kishion and En-gannim. The name En-gannim means "spring of gardens," describing a place blessed with flowing water and lush fruit orchards. Several of these towns were later set apart for the Levites, the priestly tribe that served God.

The boundary of Issachar reached Mount Tabor and Beth-shemesh, ending at the Jordan River. In total, the tribe held sixteen cities with their surrounding villages. Beth-shemesh means "house of the sun," pointing back to a time when local Canaanites worshiped the sun before Israel arrived.

This summary wraps up the cities and villages granted to the clans of Issachar. God settled them in one of the richest farming valleys in all of Canaan. Their inheritance shows God's faithful care in giving each family what they needed to thrive.

The fifth lot came out for the tribe of Asher. Asher was Jacob's son through Leah's servant Zilpah, and his descendants were now granted their own land. Their territory was located along the northwest coast of the Promised Land.

Asher's territory included several important towns and reached Mount Carmel on the southwest. Mount Carmel was a lush, green ridge rising above the sea, famous for its beauty and fertile soil. This rich coastal region fulfilled Jacob's blessing that Asher would produce rich food fit for royalty.
